content: Dicloxacillin is an antibiotic commonly used to treat bacterial infections caused by specific bacteria, particularly penicillinase-producing staphylococci. It works by binding to penicillin-binding proteins, which inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis, ultimately killing the bacteria. However, it is not effective against viral infections such as the common cold, influenza, or COVID-19, nor does it treat non-bacterial infections. Resistance to dicloxacillin can occur due to alterations in penicillin-binding proteins, reducing its effectiveness. Dicloxacillin is available in oral capsule forms of 250 mg and 500 mg. It is best absorbed on an empty stomach, taken with a large glass of water (at least 4 ounces or 120 milliliters) at least one hour before or two hours after meals. Patients should remain upright while taking the medication and avoid lying down or taking it immediately before bedtime. Common side effects of dicloxacillin include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and a black hairy tongue. Serious side effects, though less common, include severe allergic reactions, antibiotic-associated diarrhea caused by Clostridioides difficile (C. diff), seizures, kidney damage, blood disorders, and liver damage. Symptoms of severe allergic reactions may include breathing difficulties, wheezing, a racing heart, fever, swollen lymph nodes, facial swelling, hives, dizziness, or fainting. If these occur, the medication should be stopped immediately, and medical attention should be sought. Antibiotic-associated diarrhea can occur even up to two months after stopping the medication. Symptoms include watery diarrhea, persistent diarrhea, blood in the stool, severe stomach cramps, and fever. Seizures, though rare, may present as muscle twitching, jerking, tremors, or loss of consciousness. Kidney damage may manifest as reduced urination, swelling in the legs or feet, fatigue, chest pain, or confusion. Blood disorders, such as eosinophilia, hemolytic anemia, or neutropenia, may cause fever, pale or yellowish skin, easy bruising, frequent infections, or dizziness. Liver damage may present as nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fever, jaundice, dark urine, or light-colored stools. Patients with allergies to penicillins, cephalosporins, or imipenem should not take dicloxacillin. It is excreted in breast milk, so caution is advised for breastfeeding mothers. Pregnant women should consult their healthcare provider before use, as the effects on pregnancy are not fully known. Prolonged use may lead to superinfections, and elimination of the drug in neonates is slow, requiring caution in this population. Drug interactions should be carefully monitored. Dicloxacillin may interact with other medications, such as tetracyclines, probenecid, and warfarin. It can also reduce the effectiveness of live bacterial vaccines, such as the typhoid vaccine. Patients should inform their healthcare provider about all medications, supplements, and health conditions before starting dicloxacillin. If a dose is missed, it should be taken as soon as remembered unless it is close to the next scheduled dose. Double doses should be avoided. Completing the full prescribed course is essential to prevent antibiotic resistance. In case of an overdose, medical help should be sought immediately by contacting emergency services or a poison control center. Dicloxacillin is marketed under brand names such as Dynapen, Dycill, and Pathocil. It is a Pregnancy Category B drug, meaning controlled studies in pregnant women have not shown evidence of fetal risk. However, it should only be used under the guidance of a healthcare provider.
